subject: Joseph Stalin
overview: Born Ioseb Jughashvili, a cobbler's son in the Georgian town of Gori, Stalin went from seminary student and underground revolutionary to the ruler of the Soviet Union from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953. He forced the country through breakneck industrialization and farm collectivization, ran a system of purges, labor camps and famine that killed millions, and led the Soviet side of the war that defeated Nazi Germany. He left the USSR a nuclear-armed superpower facing the West across a divided Europe.

key_moments.title: From party clerk to sole ruler
key_moments.text: In 1922 the Bolsheviks made Stalin **General Secretary** of the Communist Party, a post others saw as administrative paperwork but which let him decide who got appointed where. A dying **Vladimir Lenin** dictated notes, later known as **Lenin's Testament**, warning that Stalin was too rude and should be removed from the job. After Lenin died in 1924, Stalin allied first with one faction and then another to sideline his rivals, above all **Leon Trotsky**, who was expelled from the party in 1927 and from the country in 1929. The man Trotsky had dismissed as a mediocrity had used the dullest office in the party to take the whole of it.
claims: Joseph Stalin became General Secretary of the Communist Party in 1922.
Vladimir Lenin's Testament recommended removing Joseph Stalin from the post of General Secretary.
Vladimir Lenin died in 1924.
Leon Trotsky was expelled from the Communist Party in 1927 and deported from the Soviet Union in 1929.

key_moments.title: Five-Year Plans and collectivization
key_moments.text: Stalin launched the **first Five-Year Plan** in 1928 to turn a peasant country into an industrial power, building steel towns such as **Magnitogorsk** and huge dams and factories at enormous human cost. To feed the cities and pay for machinery, peasants were forced into **collective farms**; better-off farmers labeled "kulaks" were deported or shot, and many villagers slaughtered their own livestock rather than hand it over. Grain requisitions continued as harvests failed, and the **Soviet famine of 1932–1933**, most severe in Ukraine and Kazakhstan, killed an estimated 5.5 to 8.7 million people. In Ukraine it is remembered as the **Holodomor**; whether it amounted to genocide is still debated among historians and governments.
claims: The first Soviet Five-Year Plan began in 1928.
Joseph Stalin's government forced Soviet peasants into collective farms and deported peasants labeled kulaks.
The Soviet famine of 1932–1933 hit Ukraine and Kazakhstan especially hard.
Estimates of deaths in the Soviet famine of 1932–1933 range from about 5.5 to 8.7 million.
Historians and governments disagree over whether the Holodomor constituted genocide.

key_moments.title: The Great Purge
key_moments.text: After the assassination of Leningrad party boss **Sergei Kirov** in 1934, Stalin's secret police turned on suspected enemies everywhere. Public **Moscow Trials** saw veteran Bolsheviks such as **Grigory Zinoviev**, **Lev Kamenev** and **Nikolai Bukharin** confess to fantastic plots before being shot, while the Red Army lost much of its senior command, including Marshal **Mikhail Tukhachevsky**. Historians estimate that roughly 680,000 to 750,000 people were executed in 1937–1938 alone, with hundreds of thousands more sent to the **Gulag** labor camps. Even the purgers were not safe: NKVD chief **Nikolai Yezhov**, whose name gave the worst years the label "Yezhovshchina", was himself arrested and shot.
claims: Sergei Kirov was assassinated in 1934.
Grigory Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev and Nikolai Bukharin were defendants in the Moscow Trials and were executed.
Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky was executed during the Great Purge.
An estimated 680,000 to 750,000 people were executed during the Great Purge of 1937–1938.
NKVD chief Nikolai Yezhov was himself arrested and executed.

key_moments.title: Pact with Hitler, then war against him
key_moments.text: In August 1939 Stalin's foreign minister **Vyacheslav Molotov** signed the **Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact** with Nazi Germany, secretly dividing Eastern Europe and letting the USSR occupy eastern Poland and the Baltic states. Stalin ignored repeated warnings of attack, and when Germany invaded on **22 June 1941** the Red Army suffered catastrophic losses. The Soviets held at Moscow, won at **Stalingrad** in early 1943, and took **Berlin** in May 1945, at the cost of an estimated 20 to 27 million Soviet lives. At **Yalta** in February 1945, Stalin sat with **Churchill** and **Roosevelt** to shape postwar Europe, and the zone his armies occupied became the Soviet bloc.
claims: The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact between the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany was signed in August 1939.
The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact contained a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence.
Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941.
Soviet deaths in the Second World War are estimated at roughly 20 to 27 million.
Joseph Stalin met Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt at the Yalta Conference in February 1945.

deep_facts.text: Before he was a revolutionary, the future dictator was a published romantic poet. As a teenage seminarian in Tiflis, young Jughashvili had several Georgian-language poems printed in the newspaper **Iveria**, edited by the writer and nationalist **Ilia Chavchavadze**, and one of them was later included in a Georgian anthology. The verses were about moonlight, homeland and the nobility of the poet, as far from the language of the Gulag as could be imagined.
claims: Joseph Stalin published poems in Georgian as a young man.
Joseph Stalin's youthful poems appeared in the newspaper Iveria, edited by Ilia Chavchavadze.
One of Joseph Stalin's youthful poems was later included in a Georgian anthology.

deep_facts.text: Stalin's only regular paid job outside politics was as a weather recorder. After leaving the seminary, he worked for a time at the **Tiflis Observatory**, taking meteorological readings, before police raids on the revolutionary underground pushed him into hiding and a life of strikes, arrests and Siberian exile.
claims: Joseph Stalin worked at the Tiflis Observatory after leaving the seminary.
Joseph Stalin's work at the Tiflis Observatory involved meteorological observations.
Joseph Stalin went underground after a police crackdown on revolutionaries in Tiflis.

deep_facts.text: Stalin's eldest son, **Yakov Dzhugashvili**, an artillery officer, was captured by the Germans in July 1941. After Stalingrad, the Germans reportedly offered to exchange him for Field Marshal **Friedrich Paulus**, and Stalin reportedly refused, saying he would not trade a marshal for a lieutenant. Yakov died in **Sachsenhausen concentration camp** in 1943, shot by a guard after running at the electrified fence.
claims: Yakov Dzhugashvili, Joseph Stalin's eldest son, was captured by the Germans in 1941.
Joseph Stalin reportedly refused a German offer to exchange Yakov Dzhugashvili for Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus.
Yakov Dzhugashvili died in Sachsenhausen concentration camp in 1943.

connections.name: Vladimir Lenin
connections.connection: Bolshevik leader whose Testament urged that Stalin be removed as General Secretary, a warning the party ignored.

connections.name: Leon Trotsky
connections.connection: Stalin's chief rival for power, expelled in 1929 and assassinated in Mexico by a Soviet agent in 1940.

connections.name: Adolf Hitler
connections.connection: Signed the 1939 non-aggression pact with Stalin, then broke it by invading the Soviet Union in June 1941.

connections.name: October Revolution
connections.connection: The 1917 Bolshevik seizure of power that created the state Stalin would come to rule.

connections.name: Great Purge
connections.connection: The 1936–1938 campaign of show trials and mass executions Stalin directed against real and imagined enemies.

connections.name: Eastern Front (World War II)
connections.connection: The Soviet-German war Stalin led as supreme commander from 1941 to the capture of Berlin in 1945.

connections.name: Battle of Stalingrad
connections.connection: Fought over the city bearing Stalin's name, it ended in early 1943 with the surrender of Paulus's Sixth Army.

connections.name: Cold War
connections.connection: Grew out of Stalin's postwar grip on Eastern Europe, including the 1948–1949 Berlin Blockade.

connections.name: Nikita Khrushchev
connections.connection: Stalin's successor, who denounced his crimes in the 1956 Secret Speech.

connections.name: Winston Churchill
connections.connection: Wartime ally who met Stalin at Tehran and Yalta and later warned of an Iron Curtain across Europe.

connections.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
connections.connection: US president who negotiated with Stalin at the Tehran and Yalta conferences.

connections.name: Lavrentiy Beria
connections.connection: Stalin's secret police chief from 1938, who ran the Gulag and the Soviet atomic bomb project.
